title: Advanced competitive programming
goal: Sharpen problem solving well beyond interview level through regular contests, harder techniques and upsolving. This phase runs in parallel with the others and is optional for a job but the surest path to elite algorithmic skill.
when: Months 6 to 24 (runs alongside the other phases)

steps.title: Algorithm templates (DSU, Fenwick tree, Dijkstra, KMP)
steps.note: Retype each from memory until you can write it in under five minutes.

steps.title: Codeforces
steps.note: Rated rounds roughly weekly. Always upsolve: read the editorial for the first problem you could not solve and re-implement it the next day.

steps.title: AtCoder
steps.note: High-quality problems; the ABC and ARC contests are excellent for steady growth.

steps.title: Codeforces EDU
steps.note: Step-by-step courses on segment trees, binary search and more, with practice problems.

steps.title: cp-algorithms
steps.note: The reference for every advanced algorithm you will need.

steps.title: Trees, segment trees, advanced DP, graphs II, strings II, geometry and contest strategy
steps.note: CP modules 16 to 26 are not written on this site yet (modules 11 to 15 cover Dijkstra, union-find, spanning trees, topological sort, Bellman-Ford, segment and Fenwick trees, knapsack, coin change, LIS, edit distance, LCA, KMP and the Z-function only). Learn them from cp-algorithms and Codeforces EDU, and use the pattern library to connect them to the signals you already know.

steps.title: A contest-and-upsolve habit with a rating target
steps.brief: Compete in at least two rated contests a month. After each, upsolve at least two problems and add the technique to a personal notebook with the signal that reveals it. Track your rating every month.
steps.deliverable: A public or private log of contests, upsolves and rating, with targets of about 1600, then 1900, then 2100 or higher over time.

exit: You reach about 1600 on Codeforces, then keep climbing at a steady, measured pace.
You can implement DSU, a Fenwick tree and Dijkstra from memory without looking anything up.
You upsolve every contest and can say what signal you missed in the problems you failed.
